abstract: This paper presents the first large-scale study of image-based political misinformation on Facebook. Drawing on more than 13 million posts from over 14,000 pages and 11,000 public groups collected during the run-up to the 2020 U.S. election, the authors use computational methods to identify duplicate images and political figures. They find that a substantial share of political images contained misinformation, highlighting a form of misinformation that has been understudied relative to text and links.
key_claims: Image-based political misinformation is prevalent on Facebook and constitutes a significant, understudied component of the misinformation ecosystem.
Roughly a quarter of sampled political images on Facebook contained misinformation.
Studying visual content is essential to understanding political misinformation, which prior work focused mostly on text and links has largely overlooked.
methods: Large-scale data collection of 13,723,654 posts from 14,532 pages and 11,454 public groups between August and October 2020, covering nearly all engagement with U.S. public political content on Facebook.
Perceptual hashing to identify duplicate images across the corpus.
Computer vision techniques to detect and identify political figures in images.
Manual coding of a sample of 1,000 political images to assess the prevalence of misinformation.
findings: Twenty-three percent of the sampled political images (N = 1,000) contained misinformation.
Image-based misinformation is widespread within U.S. public political content on Facebook during the 2020 election period.
contributions: First large-scale empirical study of image-based political misinformation on Facebook.
Demonstrates the application of perceptual hashing and computer vision to detect duplicate images and political figures at scale.
Provides an empirical estimate of the prevalence of misinformation in political images, extending the misinformation literature beyond text and links.
framing: The paper positions itself within research on political misinformation and social media, arguing that scholarship has focused predominantly on textual and link-based content while neglecting visual media. It contributes a computational, image-centered approach to studying misinformation dynamics on major platforms.
